{
    "id": "14-security/agent-skill-security-audit",
    "title": "Agent Skill Security Audit",
    "category": "14-security",
    "level": "advanced",
    "stability": "experimental",
    "tags": [],
    "description": "Audit an agent skill and its bundled resources before installation or execution, checking declared behavior, permissions, credential access, network egress, obfuscation, and sandbox requirements.",
    "body": "Agent Skill Security Audit Description An agent skill is executable trust-boundary content when it contains instructions, scripts, hooks, references, or tool permissions. Audit the complete skill package before installation or execution rather than trusting its description or publisher metadata. The audit is primarily static and compares declared behavior with the actual SKILL.md instructions and every bundled executable/resource file. Check for unexpected permission grants, credential reads, network egress, obfuscated content, hidden behavior, unsafe hooks, and mismatch between advertised and observable behavior. Dynamic analysis is optional and must run only in an isolated sandbox with synthetic or no credentials, bounded resources, controlled network access, and explicit teardown. An audit result is evidence for a trust decision; it is not a guarantee that a skill is benign. Inputs / Outputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---:|---| | skillroot | path | yes | Root directory containing the skill manifest and bundled resources | | declaredpermissions | list | no | Permissions/tools explicitly declared by the skill or host metadata | | runtimepolicy | object | no | Sandbox, filesystem, network, credential, and execution constraints | | auditmode | enum | yes | static or sandboxed | Output is a structured audit record containing findings, evidence locations, severity, confidence, declared-vs-observed deltas, sandbox requirements, and a disposition such as allow, review , or deny. Audit Procedure 1. Parse frontmatter and record declared name, purpose, permissions, compatibility, and provenance. 2. Inventory SKILL.md, scripts, hooks, binaries, configuration, references, and generated files under the skill root. 3. Compare advertised behavior with actual instructions and executable content. 4. Identify credential and sensitive-file access, including environment variables, SSH material, cloud credentials, token stores, and unrelated user data. 5. Identify network destinations and egress mechanisms. Treat undeclared network access as a finding requiring review. 6. Inspect for shell/process execution, package installation, dynamic code loading, obfuscation, encoded payloads, persistence, or attempts to hide behavior from the user. 7. Compare declared tool permissions with the minimum permissions required by observed behavior. 8. Record exact evidence locations and never treat absence of a detected pattern as proof of safety. 9. If dynamic analysis is required, run only in an isolated sandbox with synthetic credentials, bounded resources, controlled egress, and no access to the auditor real environment. 10. Produce a fail-closed disposition when high-confidence critical behavior is incompatible with the declared purpose or execution policy. Runnable Example This example is a bounded static signal detector, not a malware detector. Production audits need language-aware analysis, archive/binary handling, symlink controls, policy evaluation, and reproducible evidence capture. Failure Modes | Failure | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Trusting metadata | Description differs from bundled behavior | Audit executable/resource contents and record declared-vs-observed deltas | | Credential exposure | Skill reads real secrets or credential stores | Deny or isolate access; use synthetic credentials for dynamic testing | | Hidden egress | Network access is not declared or constrained | Default to no network and allow only policy-approved destinations | | Permission overreach | Skill requests tools broader than its purpose | Apply least privilege and require explicit review for elevated permissions | | Obfuscation | Encoded/dynamic content hides behavior | Flag for manual/static analysis and preserve exact evidence location | | Sandbox escape | Dynamic test reaches the host | Use a maintained isolated runtime with resource, filesystem, and network controls | | False negative | Static checks miss behavior | Treat audit output as evidence, not a safety guarantee; use layered controls | | False positive | Benign implementation matches a heuristic | Record confidence and require contextual review rather than automatic condemnation | Design Rules 1. Treat every third-party skill package as untrusted input until its behavior is reviewed. 2. Audit the complete package, not only SKILL.md frontmatter. 3. Preserve provenance and exact evidence locations for every finding. 4. Compare declared permissions and behavior against the least-privilege execution policy. 5. Default dynamic analysis to synthetic/no credentials, bounded resources, and restricted network access. 6. Never claim that a static scan prove s a skill is safe. 7. Keep audit evidence separate from authorization; a passing audit does not itself grant permission to execute a skill. 8. Prefer deterministic checks for path, permission, secret, network, and package-integrity findings where practical. References - OWASP Secure Agent Playbook issue #21: https://github.com/OWASP/secure-agent-playbook/issues/21 - 2026 research on detecting malicious agent skills: https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.06547 - Skills Tree Sandboxed Execution: sandboxed-execution.md - Skills Tree Secret Scanning: secret-scanning.md Evidence Evidence status: the cited sources support the audit problem and defensive methodology. This skill does not claim complete malware detection, compliance certification, or universal safety. Related Skills - Sandboxed Execution - Secret Scanning - Permission Checking - Input Sanitization - Audit Logging Changelog | Date | Version | Change | |---|---|---| | 2026-10 | v1 | Added demand-driven contract for pre-installation and pre-execution agent-skill security auditing |"

{
    "id": "14-security/audit-logging",
    "title": "Audit Logging",
    "category": "14-security",
    "level": "advanced",
    "stability": "stable",
    "tags": [],
    "description": "Record security-relevant agent actions in a structured, tamper-evident audit trail without logging secrets or unnecessary personal data.",
    "body": "Audit Logging Description Audit logging gives an agent system an attributable record of security-relevant actions: tool calls, resource access, authorization decisions, approvals, failures, and externally visible side effects. The log should support investigation and accountability without becoming a second data-leak channel. Use structured events with stable event types, actor identity, correlation IDs, timestamps, outcome, and a minimal resource reference. Do not record API keys, passwords, session cookies, full prompts containing sensitive data, or raw tool responses by default. Inputs / Outputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---:|---| | | string | yes | Agent, service, or human identity responsible for the event | | | string | yes | Stable action name such as or | | | string | yes | Minimal resource identifier; avoid embedding sensitive payloads | | | string | yes | , , , or | | | string | no | Identifier linking related events across a workflow | | | dict | no | Non-sensitive structured context | Output is a structured audit event containing timestamp, identity, action, resource reference, outcome, and an integrity field. Runnable Example The example demonstrates an append-only hash chain primitive. A production implementation also needs protected storage, clock handling, access controls, retention policy, and key management where stronger authenticity guarantees are required. Failure Modes | Failure | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Secret leakage | Raw tool input/output is logged | Allowlist fields and redact secrets before serialization | | Unattributed action | Shared or missing actor identity | Require authenticated actor/service identity | | Broken correlation | Each component invents unrelated IDs | Propagate a workflow correlation ID | | Log tampering | Logs are writable by the workload being audited | Separate writer and reader permissions and use append-only storage | | Excessive retention | Logs become a privacy/security liability | Define retention by purpose and data class | | Clock ambiguity | Host clocks differ | Store UTC timestamps and use a trusted event ordering strategy | | High-cardinality noise | Every internal operation becomes an event | Log security-relevant state transitions, not arbitrary debug output | Design Rules 1. Treat logs as sensitive data. 2. Log decisions and outcomes rather than secrets or complete payloads. 3. Make actor and correlation identity explicit. 4. Separate operational debugging from compliance/security audit records. 5. Define retention and deletion rules before deployment. 6. Test that denied actions generate auditable events. 7. Never treat a hash chain alone as proof of external authenticity. References - OWASP Logging Cheat Sheet: ht tps://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/LoggingCheatSheet.html - NIST AI Risk Management Framework: https://www.nist.gov/itl/ai-risk-management-framework - Python documentation: https://docs.python.org/3/library/hashlib.html Evidence Evidence status: implementation guidance is grounded in the cited security guidance; no compliance certification or performance claim is made. Related Skills - Human In Loop - Permission Checking - Secret Scanning Changelog | Date | Version | Change | |---|---|---| | 2025-03 | v1 | Initial stub | | 2026-10 | v2 | Added structured event contract, tamper-evident example, failure modes, and evidence references |"

{

    "title": "Container Escape Detection",
    "category": "14-security",
    "level": "advanced",
    "stability": "experimental",
    "tags": [],
    "description": "Detect container breakout attempts by monitoring privileged operations, namespace and capability anomalies, and kernel interface abuse from inside and around the container runtime.",
    "body": "Container Escape Detection Category: Security | Level: advanced | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description Container isolation is a soft boundary that attackers probe before they break it. The skill covers baseline of legitimate container behavior, then watching for the escape signatures: unexpected capability use, namespace and cgroup tampering, host filesystem mounts, kernel module loading, and device node access. Detections carry the workload identity so an event can be tied to a specific deployment, not just a host. When to Use Use when containerized workloads, especially those running untrusted or third-party code, must be monitored for breakout attempts toward the host. Do not assume the container image is trusted because it passed admission control. Escapes frequently come from exploited application code inside an approved image. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | Syscall, capability, and namespace events from the container runtime | | | | Yes | Normal behavior profile per workload: allowed syscalls and mounts | | | | No | (default) or for cross-node correlation | Procedure 1. Establish the per-workload baseline: syscalls, capabilities, mounts, and device access in normal operation. 2. Stream runtime events and attribute each to a workload identity and node. 3. Flag privileged deviations: capability escalation, namespace switching, and host path mounts. 4. Correlate across nodes for lateral signat ures when fleet scope is enabled. 5. Score detections by proximity to the host boundary: what a successful escape would reach. 6. Emit detections with the event chain, workload identity, and containment recommendation. Outputs | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | Escape attempts with event chains and proximity scoring | | | | Per-workload deviations from normal behavior | | | | Suggested node and workload isolation steps | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Privileged-legitimate confusion | Sidecar containers legally use high capabilities | Baseline per workload, not per node | | Kernel-level events missed | Runtime instrumentation too shallow | Instrument at the syscall or eBPF layer | | Escape already complete | Detection tuned only for attempts | Watch for post-escape signatures such as host process spawning | | Fleet-wide blind spot | Per-node alerts miss lateral movement | Correlate at fleet scope for shared tactics | | Alert fatigue | No scoring, every anomaly equal | Score by proximity to the host boundary | Security and Authority Boundary Escape detections imply compromised workloads. Treat them as live incidents: preserve forensic evidence, isolate nodes before investigation, and do not trust container-local logs after an escape is confirmed, because the attacker controls that plane. Evidence This skill is grounded in dated public implementation references: 1. The Falco runtime security project for container and syscall monitoring (https://github.com/falcosecurity/falco). 2. The Trivy vulnerability and misconfiguration scanner for containers (https://github.com/aquasecurity/trivy). {
    "id": "14-security/dependency-integrity-verification",
    "title": "Dependency Integrity Verification",
    "category": "14-security",
    "level": "intermediate",
    "stability": "experimental",
    "tags": [],
    "description": "Verify third-party package artifacts against pinned digests, signatures, and provenance attestations before installation so the build consumes exactly the artifacts that were reviewed.",
    "body": "Dependency Integrity Verification Category: Security | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description A dependency declaration names what you want; the artifact that arrives is what you run. Integrity verification closes that gap: versions pinned to exact hashes, digests recomputed at install time, signatures checked against a known identity, and provenance attestations matched to the build that produced the artifact. Anything that cannot be verified is rejected rather than installed and inspected later. When to Use Use before installing any third-party package in build, CI, or runtime environments — especially in automated pipelines that install without a human reading the output. Do not treat integrity verification as vulnerability scanning: a verified artifact is exactly the reviewed bytes, which can still contain a reviewed vulnerability. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | The dependency to install | | | | Yes | The pinned hash from the reviewed lockfile | | | | No | Detached signature over the artifact | | | | No | Build provenance statement for the artifact | Procedure 1. Pin exact versions with hashes in the lockfile; floating ranges bypass review by construction. 2. Fetch the artifact and recompute its digest locally; never trust the registry's advertised hash alone. 3. When a signature is available, verify it against a pinned signing identity, not a key fetch ed at verify time. 4. When provenance is available, check that the attestation's build matches the expected source and workflow. 5. Reject on any mismatch — digest, signature, or provenance — and fail the install. 6. Record the verification result (package, digest, verdict) so the decision is auditable later. Outputs | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | Whether the artifact matched its pinned integrity data | | | | First failed check when rejected | | | | Package, version, digest, and verdict for the audit trail | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Floating versions | ranges install whatever resolves today | Pin exact versions with hashes in the lockfile | | Registry substitution | Artifact swapped between resolve and install | Recompute the digest at install time | | Keys fetched at verify time | Signing key taken from the channel it vouches for | Pin the signing identity independently | | CI cache poisoning | Cached artifacts skip verification | Verify after cache restore, not only on download | | Mirror drift | Internal mirror serving different bytes | Verify digests from mirrors exactly like upstream | Security and Authority Boundary Integrity verification proves the artifact is the one that was attested; it says nothing about the safety or quality o f the code inside. Vulnerability scanning, license review, and human review remain separate, mandatory steps. Evidence This skill is grounded in dated public implementation references: 1. Wikipedia's overview of supply chain attacks on software distribution (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supplychainattack). 2. The Sigstore documentation on artifact signing and verification (https://docs.sigstore.dev/). Honest boundary: these are implementation references, not adoption or demand evidence; this entry was added under the owner-directed corpus expansion recorded in , and no demand signal is claimed for it. Related Skills - Secret Scanning — the paired check that no credentials ride along with the code. - Sandboxed Execution — containment for artifacts that pass verification but stay unproven in behavior. {
    "id": "14-security/forensic-log-reconstruction",
    "title": "Forensic Log Reconstruction",
    "category": "14-security",
    "level": "advanced",
    "stability": "experimental",
    "tags": [],
    "description": "Rebuild a coherent incident timeline from partial, overlapping, and clock-skewed logs, producing an evidence-backed sequence with provenance and stated confidence per event.",
    "body": "Forensic Log Reconstruction Category: Security | Level: advanced | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description Incident logs never line up: clocks drift, sources overlap or gap, and formats disagree. The skill covers collecting logs from all relevant sources into an immutable evidence store, normalizing timestamps against a common clock with skew estimates, ordering events with uncertainty bounds rather than false precision, and attributing each reconstructed event to its source lines. The timeline is the deliverable, and every entry carries its evidence. When to Use Use when an incident must be understood from heterogeneous logs: what happened, in what order, and with what evidence supporting each claim. Do not merge logs by raw timestamp. Clock skew between sources routinely reorders cause and effect, and a wrong order is worse than an honest uncertainty range. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | Logs with source, format, and observed or assumed clock offset | | | | Yes | Time range and assets in scope | | | | No | The reference clock events are normalized against | Procedure 1. Collect all in-scope logs into an append-only evidence store with source provenance. 2. Parse each source into a common event record: time, actor, action, and target. 3. Estimate per-source clock skew using handshake artifacts or known anchor events. 4. Normalize timestamps against the clock authority, carrying skew bounds as uncertainty. 5. Order events i nto a timeline, marking where uncertainty leaves the order ambiguous. 6. Attribute every timeline entry to its source lines so any claim can be re-verified. Outputs | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | Ordered incident events with uncertainty bounds and provenance | | | | Orderings that cannot be resolved within skew bounds | | | | Map from timeline entries to source log lines | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | False chronological precision | Skewed clocks treated as truth | Carry skew bounds and mark ambiguous order | | Missing middle | A source gap read as attacker dwell time | Mark gaps explicitly with their cause | | Log tampering undetected | No integrity check before analysis | Hash sources on collection and verify before use | | Timezone chaos | Sources mix local and UTC stamps | Normalize to a single clock authority first | | Unattributed conclusions | Timeline claims with no source lines | Require provenance per entry before publishing | Security and Authority Boundary Forensic timelines are legal-grade evidence in many incidents. Preserve originals immutably, document the chain of custody for every source, and never publish an incident timeline that attributes actions to individuals without direct evidence. Evidence This skill is grounded in dated public implementation references: 1. The NIST guide to integrating forensic techniques i nto incident response (https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/sp/800/86/final). 2. The Wikipedia article on computer forensics (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Computer_forensics). Honest boundary: these are implementation references, not adoption or demand evidence; this entry was added under the owner-directed corpus expansion recorded in , and no demand signal is claimed for it.     "stability": "stable",

    "description": "Triage potentially harmful agent inputs and outputs with explicit categories, thresholds, and escalation paths before high-impact actions.",
    "body": "Harm Detection Description Harm detection is a safety gate that classifies content or planned actions against an explicitly defined risk policy before an agent acts or responds.     "body": "JWT Validation Category: Security | Level: advanced | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description A JWT is three base64url parts and a lot of trust. Skipping the verification order — algorithm, signature, then claims — is how alg=none and algorithm-confusion attacks happen. This skill defines validation as a fail-closed sequence: pin the expected algorithm, verify the signature with a constant-time comparison, then evaluate claims (expiry, audience, issuer) with an injectable clock. When to Use Use whenever an agent or service accepts a JWT as evidence of identity or authorization, before any decision is made on its contents. Do not use JWTs as long-term session storage; validation is per-request evidence, and revocation needs server-side state. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | The compact serialized JWT | | | | Yes | The verification key for the pinned algorithm | | | | Yes | The single algorithm accepted; anything else is rejected | | | | No | Injectable clock for expiry claim evaluation | Procedure 1. Pin the expected algorithm in configuration; accept only that value from the token header. 2. Reject tokens whose header declares a different algorithm, a missing algorithm, or none — before any signature math runs. 3. Verify the signature over the exact signing input (header.payload) with a constant-time comparison. 4. Only after the signature holds, parse the payload and evaluate claims: expiry against the injected clock, audience, issuer. 5. Fail closed on every check; a token that fails any step is rejected without partial trust. 6. Log the validation outcome — verified or rejected with reason — without logging the token itself. 7. Never decode the payload for authorization before the signature check passes; unsigned payload is attacker input.     "description": "Scope every agent action to the minimum permission set the current step needs, with deny-by-default grants, explicit expiry, and per-action audit records so lateral movement stays contained.",
    "body": "Least-Privilege Scoping Category: Security | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description A credential that can do everything will eventually do something you did not intend. Least-privilege scoping treats authorization as a narrow, expiring grant instead of ambient power: each step names the capability and resources it needs, receives exactly that, and loses it on completion. Deny-by-default evaluation, per-grant expiry, and revocation mean a compromised step can only reach what that step was already allowed to touch. When to Use Use when an agent or automation holds credentials that can read, write, or delete beyond the single action it is performing — tool tokens, cloud roles, or API scopes. Do not use as a substitute for permission checks at the point of use; scoping narrows what a grant covers, and each call still needs its own decision. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | The capability the step wants to invoke | | | | Yes | The specific objects the action targets | | | | Yes | The standing policy grants are checked against | | | | No | Lifetime of the grant; defaults to the step boundary | Procedure 1. Start from deny-by-default: an unlisted action is rejected before any tool call is attempted. 2. Enumerate the exact capability and resource IDs the step needs; wildcard scopes require explicit justification. 3. Check the request against the standing policy, then issue a grant scoped to those resources with an expiry. 4. Evaluate each subsequent tool call against the active grant — resource by resource, not by coarse role. 5. Revoke the grant at step completion, and treat any post-revocation call as a policy violation to log. 6. Record issued grants and their use in an audit trail that answers: who, what scope, which resources, how long. A perfectly scoped grant can still perform a wrong action — purpose review and destructive-action approval remain separate, human-owned checks. {
    "id": "14-security/password-hashing",
    "title": "Password Hashing",
    "category": "14-security",
    "level": "basic",

    "description": "Store passwords as salted, iterated hashes with a declared cost parameter and constant-time verification so credential material is never stored in recoverable form.",
    "body": "Password Hashing Category: Security | Level: basic | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description A password stored in plaintext is a breach waiting for a date; a password hashed once without salt is a rainbow-table lookup. This skill defines credential storage as a contract: a per-user random salt, a slow memory-hard or iterated hash function, a declared cost parameter, and constant-time comparison on verification. The stored record keeps the algorithm and cost with the digest so migration to stronger parameters is possible. When to Use Use whenever a system stores a user-provided secret for later verification — passwords, PINs, API secrets — and must never recover the plaintext. Do not use for non-recoverable-but-high-entropy tokens like OAuth client secrets; those can be stored as plain fast hashes since entropy does the work. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | The secret being stored or verified | | | | Yes | Per-user random salt, generated at first store | | | | Yes | Iteration count or hardness parameter, declared in policy | | | | Yes | The existing record for verification | Procedure 1. Generate a fresh random salt per credential at first store; reuse of salts across users is a defect. 2. Derive the digest with a salted slow hash and a cost parameter declared in policy, never chosen per call. 3. Store the salt, cost, and algorithm identifier alongside the digest so verification and migration are unambiguous. 4. Verify by re-deriving with the stored paramete rs and comparing in constant time; early-exit comparison leaks timing. 5. Reject passwords below the declared minimum entropy policy before hashing; the hash cannot repair a weak secret. 6. Rehash transparently on next successful login when the policy cost rises, and record the migration. 7. Never log the password, its digest, or the comparison result beyond pass/fail. Outputs | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | The stored credential record | | | | Constant-time comparison result | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Rainbow-table recovery | Digests computed without per-user salt | Generate a random salt per credential | | Cost stagnation | Iteration count frozen as hardware speeds up | Raise the policy cost and rehash on next login | | Timing leaks | Comparison short-circuits on first mismatch | Compare derived digests in constant time | | Weak secrets admitted | Short passwords hashed as-is | Enforce a minimum-length and entropy policy before hashing | | Digest logging | Credential records written to logs | Log only pass/fail outcomes, never the material | Security and Authority Boundary Hashing protects stored credentials, not the channel or the policy: transport still needs TLS, verification still needs rate limiting, and a verified password grants only what its account’s policy allows.     "body": "Privilege Escalation Detection Category: Security | Level: advanced | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description Privilege escalation rarely breaks in one step; it chains small permission wins. The skill covers modeling the legitimate paths by which accounts and processes gain privilege in an environment, then watching for events that fall outside those paths: unexpected group membership changes, service account logins on new hosts, elevation anomalies, and token manipulation. Detections are chains, so the output correlates events rather than raising single-line alerts. When to Use Use when authorization-relevant logs must be monitored for accounts or processes obtaining more privilege than their documented paths allow. Do not alert on every permission change. Without a model of legitimate paths, the detection floods operators and real escalations hide in the noise. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | Authentication and authorization events with timestamps and principals | | | | Yes | Documented legitimate privilege change paths per role and host | | | | No | Correlation window in minutes for chaining related events | Procedure 1. Ingest authentication and authorization logs and normalize principals, actions, and targets. 2. Load the permission baseline: who may grant what, through which documented paths. 3. Match each event against the baseline; unmatched events are candidate deviations. 4. Correlate candidates within the window into chains: grant, use, and pe rsist sequences. 5. Score chains by blast radius: what the gained privilege reaches. 6. Emit detections with the full chain, the baseline clause violated, and recommended response. Outputs | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | Escalation chains with events, violated baseline clause, and score | | | | Legitimate-but-unmodeled paths that need baseline updates | | | | Suggested containment per detection | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Alert flooding | No baseline, so every change is suspicious | Model legitimate paths first, then deviate | | Missed slow chains | Events days apart never correlated | Add long-window correlation for persistence stages | | Service account blind spots | Shared accounts break principal identity | Attribute actions to workload identity where possible | | Baseline staleness | New admin processes unmodeled | Review baseline gaps emitted by the detection loop | | Single-event alerts | Chains scored as isolated lines | Score and raise chains, not isolated events | Security and Authority Boundary Escalation detections name accounts and hosts that may already be compromised.     "description": "Execute untrusted agent-generated code inside a separately enforced isolation boundary with resource, filesystem, network, and timeout controls.",
    "body": "Sandboxed Execution Description Sandboxed execution separates untrusted code from the agent host and limits what the code can read, write, execute, and connect to. A timeout alone is not a sandbox. Production isolation should be enforced by an operating-system, container, VM, or dedicated execution service boundary. Treat the sandbox policy as part of the security contract: filesystem visibility, network egress, CPU/memory limits, process privileges, runtime image, and cleanup must all be explicit. It is not a security sandbox and must not be used as isolation for hostile code without an additional OS/container/VM boundary. Failure Modes | Failure | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Host escape | Weak isolation boundary | Use a maintained container/VM runtime and least privilege | | Network exfiltration | Unrestricted egress | Default to no network; allow only required destinations | | Resource exhaustion | CPU/memory/process abuse | Enforce hard resource quotas outside the guest process | | Filesystem exposure | Host paths mounted into the sandbox | Use an isolated workspace and read-only mounts where possible | | Dependency attack | Untrusted packages installed at runtime | Use pinned images/packages and controlled registries | | Cleanup failure | Processes survive after timeout | Kill the process tree and verify cleanup | Design Rules - Do not call or on untrusted input in the agent process. - Do not treat a Python timeout as a security boundary. - Default network access to disabled. - Use non-root execution and a minimal runtime image. - Apply resource limits outside the untrusted process. - Delete temporary state after execution and verify cleanup. - Keep sandbox credentials separate from host credentials. {
    "id": "14-security/session-management",
    "title": "Session Management",
    "category": "14-security",
    "level": "intermediate",
    "stability": "experimental",
    "tags": [],
    "description": "Create, rotate, and expire agent sessions with server-side state, opaque identifiers, and re-authentication on privilege change so identity evidence stays fresh instead of indefinitely trusted.",
    "body": "Session Management Category: Security | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description A session is a server-side record plus a token that points at it; the token is evidence, not the identity itself. Session management keeps the record authoritative: opaque identifiers, rotation on login and privilege change, idle plus absolute expiry, and invalidation that actually invalidates. A leaked old token stops working because the record moved on — not because someone hoped it would. When to Use Use when an agent or service maintains state across requests on behalf of an identity — web sessions, agent run sessions, or API tokens issued per engagement. Do not use sessions as long-term authorization storage; a session says who someone was recently, and privilege should be re-established when the risk window grows. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | Authenticated identity the session represents | | | | Yes | Max gap between requests before expiry | | | | Yes | Max total lifetime regardless of activity | | | | Yes | Server-side session state | Procedure 1. Store session state server-side; issue only an opaque, high-entropy identifier to the client. 2. Set both idle and absolute expiry; whichever fires first ends the session. 3. Rotate the identifier on login, on privilege change, and on any suspected disclosure. 4. Invalidate the server record on logout; a client-side cookie clear is not invalidatio n. 5. Require re-authentication for sensitive operations even inside a valid session. 6. Record creation, rotation, and expiry events in the audit log with actor and time. Outputs | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | Opaque identifier for the active session | | | | active, expiredidle, expiredabsolute, or revoked | | | | Session lifecycle events for auditing | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Client-side session trust | State stored where the client can edit it | Keep the record server-side; issue opaque IDs | | Eternal sessions | Only idle expiry configured | Enforce absolute TTL on top of idle timeout | | Missing rotation | Same identifier across privilege changes | Rotate on login and privilege change | | Predictable identifiers | Sequential or low-entropy session IDs | Use high-entropy random identifiers | | Logout theater | Cookie cleared client-side, record alive | Invalidate the server record on logout | Security and Authority Boundary A session carries recent identity evidence; it is not proof of continued presence or intent. Re-authentication, step-up verification, and the decision to trust a session at all remain with the identity provider and the calling service. Evidence This skill is grounded in dated public impl ementation references: 1. The OWASP Session Management Cheat Sheet (https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/SessionManagementCheat_Sheet.html). 2. MDN's reference on the Set-Cookie header and session attributes (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Headers/Set-Cookie).     "body": "Social Engineering Detection Category: Security | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description Social engineering attacks people, not code, so detection works on message patterns and process anomalies. The skill covers screening inbound communications for the classic patterns: manufactured urgency, unverifiable authority, pretext setup, and redirection to off-channel or credential capture. It flags for review rather than silently blocking, because false positives on legitimate urgent mail are costly, and it never auto-responds to a suspected attacker. When to Use Use when inbound email, chat, or support requests must be screened for phishing, pretexting, executive impersonation, and credential or payment redirection. Do not auto-reply to suspected attacks or reveal the detection. Acknowledgment teaches the attacker what worked and marks the target as monitored. Inspect links and attachments for credential capture and off-channel redirection. 4. Score the message from matched patterns and route by threshold: review, w arn, or block. 5. Escalate with the evidence: matched patterns, sender analysis, and links. 6. Never auto-respond; suspected messages are silently routed to review.     "body": "Threat Intelligence Enrichment Category: Security | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description Enrichment turns an IP or hash into context only when the source is trustworthy and current. The skill covers normalizing observables, matching them against structured feeds, attaching tactic and campaign context with source attribution, and scoring confidence with feed age and source reputation included. Feeds are treated as untrusted input: a single aggressive feed cannot dominate verdicts, and stale indicators age out. When to Use Use when alerts, logs, or user reports must be prioritized with external threat context: known actors, campaign affiliation, and observed infrastructure. Do not treat every feed as equally trustworthy. Poisoned feeds produce both false alerts and false clearance, so confidence scoring must include source reputation. Normalize observables into canonical forms: IP version handling, domain case, and hash algorithms. 2. Match against the feeds, recording every hit with its source and record timestamp. 3. Attach available context: tactics, campaign names, and related infrastructure. 4. Score confidence combining source reputation, record age, and corroboration across feeds. 5. Age out stale indicators so old intelligence cannot keep driving verdicts. 6. Emit enrichment with provenance so any verdict can be traced to its records. {
    "id": "14-security/threat-modeling",
    "title": "Threat Modeling",
    "category": "14-security",
    "level": "intermediate",
    "stability": "experimental",
    "tags": [],
    "description": "Model a system’s components against a structured threat taxonomy with per-interaction mitigations so security work is driven by an enumerated, reviewable threat list instead of ad-hoc paranoia.",
    "body": "Threat Modeling Category: Security | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description Security without enumeration becomes either paralysis or theater. Threat modeling imposes order: decompose the system into components and interactions, walk a fixed taxonomy — spoofing, tampering, repudiation, information disclosure, denial of service, elevation of privilege — per component, and record a mitigation or an explicit acceptance for every threat found. The model is the artifact; fixes are tracked against it. When to Use Use when designing or changing a system that handles untrusted input, credentials, or privileged operations, and when the security posture must be explainable to a reviewer. Do not use as a substitute for testing; a model guides where to test and review, and unverified mitigations are intentions, not protections. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | System decomposition under review | | | | Yes | Recorded threats and their handling per component | | | | Yes | The threat classes walked per component | Procedure 1. Decompose the system into components and their interactions before naming a single threat. 2. Walk the declared taxonomy for every component, in a fixed order, so classes are never skipped silently. 3. Record each threat with its entry point and a mitigation, or an explicit accepted-risk note — never an empty cell. 4. Treat missing mitigations as findings with ow ners and deadlines, not as future hopes. 5. Update the model whenever the decomposition changes; a model of the old system protects nothing. 6. Re-test mitigations that the model claims; an untested mitigation is a documented guess. Outputs | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | Enumerated threats and their handling status | | | | Taxonomy classes with no recorded interaction | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Taxonomy skipping | Only familiar threat classes examined | Walk the full taxonomy per component in fixed order | | Empty-cell acceptance | Threats noted without mitigation or decision | Require a mitigation or an explicit accepted-risk note | | Stale model | System changed, model unchanged | Re-model on every decomposition change | | Untested mitigations | Controls recorded but never verified | Track mitigations as testable findings with owners | | Paralysis inversion | Enumeration replaces remediation | Every finding needs an owner and a de adline | Security and Authority Boundary The model itself is sensitive: it enumerates exactly where the system is soft. Treat threat models as need-to-know artifacts and protect them with the same care as the codebase. Evidence This skill is grounded in dated public implementation references: 1. Honest boundary: these are implementation references, not adoption or demand evidence; this entry was added under the owner-directed corpus expansion recorded in , and no demand signal is claimed for it.     "body": "Vulnerability Triage Category: Security | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description Triage converts a raw finding list into a fix order. The skill covers normalizing findings into a common record, scoring with a stated rubric such as CVSS adjusted for exploit maturity and asset exposure, grouping duplicates and root causes, and emitting a ranked queue with the reasoning attached. The rubric is recorded so two analysts reach the same order from the same inputs. When to Use Use when scanner output, penetration test findings, or external reports must be converted into a prioritized remediation queue. Do not sort by scanner-provided severity alone. A critical on an unreachable internal host can matter less than a high on an internet-facing one, and the queue must reflect that. Normalize every finding into one record: source, asset, weakness class, and evidence. 2. Deduplicate findings that share a root cause and link them. 3. Score each unique issue with the rubric: base severity, exploit maturity, and exposure. 4. Adjust for reachability: an issue on an unreachable host is downgraded with the reason recorded. 5. Group by root cause so one fix can retire multiple finding s. 6. Emit a ranked queue with scores, rationale, and suggested fix grouping.
